title: Collections and Streams
excerpt: Collections and Streams Java's collections hold many values — List , Set , Map . Streams let you process them fluently. A stream example List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Bob", "Cara"); long count = names.stream() .filter(n -> n.length() > 3) .count(); System.out.println(count); // 2 Try filtering names that start with "A" and collecting them into a new list.

title: Object-Oriented Java: Inheritance
excerpt: OOP: Inheritance Inheritance lets a class reuse code from another. extends in action class Animal { void speak() { System.out.println("..."); } } class Dog extends Animal { @Override void speak() { System.out.println("Woof!"); } } When to use it Use inheritance when "is-a" applies: a Dog is an Animal. Otherwise prefer composition. Try making a Cat class that extends Animal .

title: Java Basics: Classes and Objects
excerpt: Java Basics Java is object-oriented — everything lives inside a class . The simplest program already shows this. Your first class public class Hello { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, Raven!"); } } Save as Hello.java , compile with javac Hello.java , run with java Hello . Variables and types String name = "Ada"; int age = 21; double pi = 3.14; boolean isStudent = true; Unlike Python, Java needs the type up front.

title: Functions and Modules
excerpt: Functions and Modules A function is a reusable recipe. A module is a file full of recipes. Defining functions def greet(name): return f"Hello, {name}!" print(greet("Raven")) Modules import math print(math.sqrt(16)) # or: from math import sqrt Try importing random and printing a random number.

title: Control Flow: if, for, while
excerpt: Control Flow Your code makes decisions with if and repeats work with for and while . if / elif / else score = 72 if score >= 90: print("A") elif score >= 60: print("Pass") else: print("Try again") Loops for i in range(5): print(i) n = 3 while n > 0: print(n) n -= 1

title: Python Basics: Syntax and Variables
excerpt: Python Basics Welcome to Python — the language behind data science, web apps, and automation. This chapter covers how Python looks and how you store values. Variables and Types name = "Ada" age = 21 pi = 3.14159 is_student = True Python figures out the type for you — no int or string declaration needed. Use type(x) to check. A mini task Try this in your editor: print(f"Hi, I am {name} and I am {age}") # What does type(pi) print?
